cards.title: CSP hardness under linear treewidth caps
cards.formal: Resolved under ETH, with the source’s structural restriction read as an upper cap: for every fixed finite constraint language Γ over a finite domain such that CSP(Γ) is NP-complete, and every fixed constant c>0, CSP(Γ) restricted to instances I with primal treewidth tw(I)≤c·n(I) has no subexponential-time algorithm. Here n(I) is the number of variables. This follows from the source’s Corollary 10 after the algebraic dichotomy was proved, together with the disjoint-copy padding used in the cited structural-CSP literature.
cards.why: Clarifies the interaction between a fixed constraint language and structural restrictions in exact algorithms. For a linear upper cap, the established reduction shows that the restriction alone cannot remove ETH hardness; finer graph-class claims require additional hypotheses.
cards.status_note: Matched the exact upper-cap interpretation against Theorem 7 and its padding proof in the AAAI precursor to the source’s 2015 citation. Read the source’s Corollary 10 and full-version question, and Bulatov’s FOCS theorem and statement of its algebraic criterion. Resolution is a direct composition of these published results, conditional on ETH, rather than a claim that a later paper explicitly announces this corollary. The full 2015 JAIR PDF was unavailable; proofs were not independently audited.

progress.text: Theorem 7 defines the linear upper-cap problem and gives the disjoint-copy reduction for general CSP.
The source proves the unrestricted fixed-language implication under the algebraic dichotomy and asks about structural restrictions.
The algebraic dichotomy is proved at FOCS. Combining it with the source’s Corollary 10 and the cited padding yields the fixed-language linear-cap conclusion.

cards.definitions:
A finite constraint language Γ is a finite list of relations on a fixed finite nonempty domain D. A relation R of arity r is a subset of Dʳ. An instance I consists of a finite set V of n variables and a finite list of constraints R(v₁,…,v_r), with R∈Γ; repeated variables in a scope are permitted. The decision task is whether some assignment a:V→D satisfies (a(v₁),…,a(v_r))∈R for every constraint. Γ and D are fixed before the instance is supplied. Variable indices and relation names are explicitly encoded in binary, and L denotes the full input bit length. NP-completeness refers to this unrestricted fixed-language decision problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, not to a language supplied as part of each input.

The primal graph has vertex set V and an undirected edge between distinct variables that occur together in a constraint. A tree decomposition consists of a finite tree with a bag B_t⊆V at each tree node, such that every graph vertex appears in at least one bag, the endpoints of each edge appear together in some bag, and the bags containing a fixed vertex induce a connected subtree. Its width is max_t |B_t|−1; treewidth is the minimum width. The input is promised to satisfy tw(I)≤c n. No decomposition has to be supplied, and the algorithm need not recognize the promise. There is no bound on the number of graph components and no connectedness promise.

The source defines subexponential solvability by an infimum of exponential rates. With the usual polynomial input overhead made explicit, it means: for every ε>0 there is a deterministic algorithm A_ε and a constant K_ε that decide every promised instance in time O(2^{ε n}L^{K_ε}). Algorithms may depend on the fixed Γ,c,ε. Their worst-case running time counts ordinary bit operations; randomness and average-case bounds are not part of this question. The claimed impossibility rules out this entire family of arbitrarily small exponential rates, and hence also rules out a single 2^{o(n)}L^{O(1)} algorithm. ETH is the assertion that 3-SAT, satisfiability of Boolean formulas with at most three literals per clause, does not admit such arbitrarily small exponential rates in its number of variables.

The phrase “bounded by Ω(n)” in the source is recovered from the structural theorem it cites: treewidth is bounded ABOVE by a function at least linear in n. The concrete form tw≤cn, for every fixed c>0, already captures the relevant hardness. If a cap b(n) is at least cn eventually, the b-cap class contains the c-cap class apart from finitely many lengths. The card does not require tw≥cn, and it does not assert hardness on every chosen graph class whose treewidth is linear. A high treewidth value alone is not a per-instance hardness claim.

The implication between the cited results is direct. For an unrestricted instance with n variables, take r=⌈1/c⌉ disjoint identical copies when c<1, and r=1 otherwise. This preserves satisfiability and the language Γ, multiplies the number of variables by the constant r, and leaves treewidth unchanged. Since tw(I)≤n−1, the result satisfies the c-cap. Thus a subexponential algorithm on that promise would give one for unrestricted CSP(Γ). This is the existing padding argument specialized to a fixed language, not a new hardness theorem for a restricted family of connected graphs.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative conditional resolution combines the unrestricted fixed-language ETH lower bound with the stated language-preserving, constant-copy reduction into the upper-cap class. The conclusion is conditional on ETH. A claim for a lower treewidth promise, one connected graph family, an exact exponential base or randomized algorithms would be a different statement.
